doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Answering services and the cartage companies
summary: Busy session players used answering services, and Hal Blaine and others pioneered drum cartage between studios.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Some of the guys were even telling me that if they had to go out of town they tried not to let people know because as a session musician if your phone rings and you don’t pick ups then —

Yeah. Well it was so busy back then, everybody had an answering service. And after every session, everybody’d be out in the hall on the — not cell phones — on the pay phones, calling their service to see what dates were booked for them the next day or the next week or that type of thing. And they’d be writing in their book. And that’s where Cartage Company started up in LA because guys like Hal Blaine, the drummer from the Wrecking Crew and those people, they had so many sessions. They may do a 10:00 session for whoever, but their 2:00 session might be a different artist in another studio. So to get the drum set from here over to the next studio, set up and miced, it was those guys who started thinking about, okay I’ll have three sets of drums. And while they’re playing that session the Cartage Companies with the big trucks would take the equipment trunks to the next studio and they would set up the drums and the engineers could mic it, so Hal Blaine could play drums over at Sunset Sound in the morning, take his lunch break, and
at 2:00 he’d be at United Western Studio with his other drum set already set up. And maybe at 6:00 it’d be the third studio with his third drum set. That’s the way it was.
